mainTopic: Rabbinic penalties for unseen damage, and blemishes on a בכור: intentional versus accidental blemishes, when a blemish counts, and who is believed about how it came about
overview: This amud begins by finishing an earlier topic. If someone made another person's טהרות impure and then died, his son does not pay, because damage you cannot see is only a rabbinic קנס, and a קנס falls only on the person who did the act. Then a new משנה tells two stories about a בכור that was blemished: a Roman official cut its ear, and children at play tore off a tail. The first time, the animal was permitted. When people copied the act on purpose, the חכמים forbade those animals. The rule is that a blemish made with the owner's intent forbids the animal, even when done indirectly (גרמא), and one made without his intent permits it. The גמרא then discusses a בכור that chased its owner and got kicked, and gives two versions of רב פפא about a kick after the chase. It also teaches that a בכור may be blemished before it is born, and that a mouth blemish that shows only when the animal cries out counts as a מום. Finally, a new משנה asks which shepherds are believed when they say a blemish was not made on purpose. רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר disagree about how to read it, and the second reading begins at the end of the amud.

steps.title: If the one who made the pure items impure dies, his son does not pay
steps.stepSummary: A ruling is quoted: if someone made another person's טהרות impure and then died, the חכמים did not penalize his son.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person made pure items impure and then died, the Sages did not penalize his son after him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a ruling that belongs to the earlier discussion about damage you cannot see. Someone made another person's pure food impure and died before paying, and his son does not have to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making food impure causes a real loss, because the food can no longer be used in purity. But nothing about the food looks different. That is why the obligation to pay is unusual, and step 3 explains why it does not pass to an heir.

keyTerms.meaning: ritually pure items (usually food kept in purity)

phrases.english: If he made pure items impure and died —
phrases.notes: The pure items belonged to someone else.

phrases.english: they did not penalize his son after him.
phrases.notes: The heir does not pay from the estate.

steps.triggerLanguage: טִימֵּא טְהָרוֹת וָמֵת — לֹא קָנְסוּ בְּנוֹ אַחֲרָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the previous page's discussion of היזק שאינו ניכר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The heir of someone who made another person's טהרות impure is not required to pay.

steps.title: Why is the son exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason the son is not penalized.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the son is exempt. This short question sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, if a father owed money for damage, his heirs pay from the estate he left. So the son's exemption needs an explanation.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the ruling in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the heir is not liable, when heirs usually pay their father's debts.

steps.title: Unseen damage is only a rabbinic penalty, and it applied only to the person who did it
steps.stepSummary: By Torah law, damage that cannot be seen is not damage. The payment is a rabbinic קנס, and the חכמים placed it only on the one who caused the damage, not on his son.
steps.simpleTranslation: Damage that is not visible is not called damage. The payment is a rabbinic penalty. The Sages penalized him, but the Sages did not penalize his son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. By Torah law there is no real debt, only a penalty from the חכמים, and that penalty was aimed only at the wrongdoer himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this were a Torah-level debt, the estate would have to pay. Since היזק שאינו ניכר is not damage by Torah law, the only obligation is a קנס דרבנן. A penalty is meant to punish the person who did wrong, so it does not pass to his innocent son.

keyTerms.meaning: damage that cannot be seen (no physical change)
a penalty imposed by the Sages

steps.whatToRemember: היזק שאינו ניכר is not damage by Torah law. The payment is a rabbinic קנס, and a קנס applies only to the person who did the act, not to his heirs.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the son is exempt because no loss happened. There was a real loss, which is why the חכמים fined the person who caused it. The point is only that a fine does not pass to heirs.

phrases.english: Damage that is not visible
is not called damage,
phrases.notes: This is by Torah law.

phrases.english: it is a rabbinic penalty —
the Sages penalized him himself,
the Sages did not penalize his son.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר לָא שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The obligation is only a rabbinic קנס, and the חכמים placed it on the wrongdoer personally, not on his heir.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Liability for היזק שאינו ניכר is a personal rabbinic penalty and is not collected from heirs.

steps.title: The official who cut the ear of a firstborn ram
steps.stepSummary: A non-Jewish official cut the ear of an old בכור. The חכמים permitted that animal. When he then cut the ears of other בכורות, the חכמים forbade them.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident with an old ram whose wool was hanging long. A Roman official saw it and asked, "What is the story with this one?" They told him, "It is a firstborn, and it may only be slaughtered if it has a blemish." He took a dagger and slit its ear. The case came before the Sages, and they permitted it. After they permitted it, he went and slit the ears of other firstborns, and the Sages forbade those.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a story. A gentile blemished a בכור, and the חכמים permitted it the first time. When he did it again on purpose to other animals, the חכמים forbade them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור in our time may only be eaten once it has a מום. The official did cut the ear on purpose, but the Jewish owners did not intend or arrange it, so the first animal was allowed. Once the חכמים had permitted it, the later cuts could no longer count as happening without the owners' knowledge, so the חכמים forbade them.

keyTerms.meaning: a firstborn male animal, holy to a כהן

steps.confusionAlert: The animal's status as a בכור never changes. The question is only whether this particular blemish allows it to be slaughtered.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
There was an incident with an old male sheep (a ram),
and its wool was long and dangling,
phrases.notes: It grew old because, as a בכור, it could not be slaughtered without a blemish.

phrases.english: and a certain official saw it and said:
What is the nature of this one?
They said to him: It is a firstborn,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינוֹ נִשְׁחָט אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן הָיָה בּוֹ מוּם.
phrases.english: and it may only be slaughtered if it has a blemish.
He took a dagger and slit its ear,
phrases.notes: The text has a corrected reading: פיגום is changed to פִּיגְיוֹם.

phrases.english: and the case came before the Sages and they permitted it,
and after they permitted it,
he went and slit the ears of other firstborns,
and they forbade them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic: blemishes made by people on a בכור.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blemish a gentile makes without the owner's prompting permits the בכור the first time. After that היתר became known, the חכמים forbade animals he blemished later.

steps.title: Children tied lambs' tails together
steps.stepSummary: Children playing tied lambs' tails together, and a בכור's tail came off. The חכמים permitted it. When people then tied the tails of other בכורות on purpose, the חכמים forbade them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once, children were playing in a field and tied the tails of lambs to each other. The tail of one of them came off, and it was a firstborn. The case came before the Sages, and they permitted it. People saw that the Sages had permitted it, so they went and tied the tails of other firstborns, and the Sages forbade those.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה tells a second, similar story. This time the blemish was made by Jewish children at play, which was clearly an accident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern repeats: the first, accidental blemish is permitted. Adults who copied it on purpose to get the animals permitted were refused.

phrases.aramaic: פַּעַם אַחַת הָיוּ תִּינוֹקוֹת מְשַׂחֲקִין בַּשָּׂדֶה,
phrases.english: Once, children were playing in the field,
and they tied the tails of lambs to each other,
and the tail of one of them was torn off,
and it was a firstborn,
and the case came before the Sages and they permitted it.
People saw that they had permitted it,
so they went and tied the tails of other firstborns,
and the Sages forbade them.

steps.triggerLanguage: פַּעַם אַחַת הָיוּ תִּינוֹקוֹת מְשַׂחֲקִין בַּשָּׂדֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story with the same result, this time involving Jewish children.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An accidental blemish made by children is accepted, but copying it on purpose is not.

steps.title: The rule: a blemish made on purpose forbids, an accidental one permits
steps.stepSummary: The משנה sums up both stories in one principle. A blemish made intentionally forbids slaughter, and one made unintentionally permits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: any blemish made on purpose makes the animal forbidden. One made not on purpose leaves it permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה turns the two stories into a general rule about intention.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What decides the case is not who caused the blemish but whether it was done deliberately, in order to make the בכור permitted. A deliberate blemish is penalized by forbidding the animal.
steps.whatToRemember: A מום made on purpose in a בכור does not permit it to be slaughtered. Only an accidental מום does.

phrases.english: This is the rule:
anything done intentionally is forbidden,
anything done unintentionally is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כֹּל שֶׁהוּא לְדַעְתּוֹ — אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the general principle out of the two stories.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Intention decides the case: a deliberate blemish forbids the בכור, and an accidental one permits it.

steps.title: Why the משנה needed the children's story too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why both stories were needed. From the gentile's case alone, we might have thought the leniency applied only because a gentile will not get into the habit of blemishing. A Jewish child might form the habit, so we might have forbidden even the first time.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says, "Another time there was..." Both stories are necessary. If we had only been taught about the gentile, we might have said he was permitted because he will not get into the habit. But a child, who might get into the habit, we might say is not permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the start of the second story and answers an unspoken question: why tell two stories that teach the same thing? This is a צריכותא, an explanation of why each case is necessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gentile has no obligation regarding בכור, so permitting his act creates no risk that he will make a habit of it. A Jewish child could grow used to blemishing בכורות, so we might have expected the חכמים to forbid even his first, accidental act. The children's story teaches that an accidental act is still permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: and it is necessary (to teach both cases)
I would say no (it is not permitted)

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the concern about forming a bad habit does not override the basic rule: an accidental מום permits the בכור even when the person who caused it is Jewish.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
"Another time there was," etc.
phrases.notes: A quote of the start of the משנה's second story.

phrases.english: And it is necessary,
for if it had taught us only about a gentile —
that is because he will not get into the habit,
but a minor, who will get into the habit —
I would say it is not permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the משנה included the second story.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: shows that each case teaches something the other does not
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only the gentile's case, we would have thought an accidental blemish by a Jewish child is forbidden because he might form a habit.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a Jewish minor's accidental blemish permits the בכור.

steps.title: Why the children's story alone would not have been enough
steps.stepSummary: This finishes the צריכותא. From the children's story alone, we might have permitted only a קטן's act, because nobody confuses a child with an adult. A gentile adult could be confused with a Jewish adult, so we might have forbidden his case. That is why both stories are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had taught us only the child's case, we would say it was permitted because people won't confuse a child with an adult. But a gentile, who could be confused with an adult Jew, we might say is not permitted. So both stories are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining why the משנה told both stories. Here it shows that the children's story alone would not have taught us the gentile's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 7 we learned that the gentile's case alone would not teach us about the child, because a child might get into a habit. Now the reverse: a child's act is clearly not an adult's, so permitting it won't mislead anyone. A gentile adult looks like any adult, so people might think a Jewish adult may also make a blemish. Each story covers a worry the other one doesn't, so both are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: to be confused / mixed up with
it is necessary (both cases had to be taught)

steps.whatToRemember: Each story protects against a different mistake. The gentile story shows that a one-time act by someone who won't form a habit is permitted. The children story shows that a child's act is permitted even though children might form habits, because no one confuses a child with an adult.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only the minor,
that is because people won't come to confuse him with an adult,
but a gentile, who might be confused with an adult (Jew) —
phrases.notes: People might think a Jewish adult may also make a blemish.

phrases.english: I might say: no, not permitted.
Therefore both are necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the צריכותא begun in step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case teaches something the other cannot
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the child's case alone, a gentile adult's blemish might be forbidden because he could be confused with a Jewish adult.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both stories are needed. Each one rules out a different stringency.

steps.title: The official's case depends on what the bystanders said
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting רב קטינא, limits the official's story. It was permitted only because they told him 'unless it HAS a blemish.' If they had said 'unless a blemish IS MADE on it,' that counts as telling him to go make one, and the animal would be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רב קטינא: They taught this only when they told him 'unless it has a blemish.' But if they told him 'unless a blemish is made on it,' it is as if they told him 'go make a blemish on it.'
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא now adds a limit to the story of the gentile official who cut the בכור's ear. The leniency depends on the exact words the Jews used when they answered him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'unless it HAS a blemish' just describes the law, so the official acted on his own. Saying 'unless a blemish IS MADE' sounds like an invitation for someone to make it. In that case the cut is like the Jews' own intentional act, and the animal is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: they only taught this (rule) when…: a limiting formula
it had a blemish (describes a state)
a blemish was made on it
go make a blemish on it

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said in the name of Rav Ketina:
They taught this only where they said to him
"(it can't be slaughtered) unless it has a blemish,"
but if they said to him
"if a blemish is made on it" —
it is like they told him
"go make a blemish on it."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns back to the official's story to limit when its leniency applies
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The official's case is permitted only if the Jews said 'unless it has a blemish.' Saying 'if a blemish is made' counts as telling him to make one, so the animal is forbidden.

steps.title: רבא: both phrasings mean the blemish happened by itself
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees with רב קטינא. Both 'it has' and 'it was made' describe a blemish that came about without the speaker doing anything. So the wording makes no difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Both mean it happened by itself. What difference does it make whether they said 'had' or 'was made'? 'Was made' also means by itself. There is no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא argues with the limit just given by רב קטינא. He says the two phrases mean the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא points out that 'was made' is passive. It does not tell anyone to do anything. Just like 'it has a blemish,' it describes the blemish as coming on its own. So in both cases the official acted on his own, and the בכור is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: now, consider: introduces a logical argument
what difference is there between… and…

steps.whatToRemember: רב קטינא says the wording 'was made' turns it into an instruction. רבא says both wordings are passive, so it is permitted either way.

phrases.english: Rava said: Now, it is by itself (either way),
what difference is there to me between "had" and "was made"?
Rather, "was made" also means by itself,
and there is no difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב קטינא's distinction between the two phrasings
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole distinction between 'היה' and 'נעשה'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'נעשה' is passive and does not tell anyone to act, so it is no different from 'היה'.

steps.title: What does the general rule come to add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that any blemish made with intent is forbidden. It then asks what extra case this general rule includes beyond the stories already told.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: anything done on purpose is forbidden. What does this come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's general rule and asks what it adds. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'זה הכלל' in a משנה is usually understood to include a case not already stated. The stories already taught direct blemishing and accidental blemishing. So the גמרא wants to know which further case the rule covers.

keyTerms.meaning: what does it come to include?

phrases.english: This is the general rule:
any (blemish) that is done with intent — is forbidden.
What does this come to include?

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כֹּל שֶׁהוּא לְדַעַת — אָסוּר. לְאֵיתוֹיֵי מַאי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's summary rule from step 6 to ask what it adds
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra case is included by the general rule 'כל שהוא לדעת אסור'?

steps.title: It includes causing a blemish indirectly
steps.stepSummary: The rule comes to include גרמא. Even if a person does not make the blemish with his own hands, but sets things up so that it happens, it counts as intentional and the animal is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include an indirect cause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the general rule adds the case of causing a blemish indirectly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think only a direct act, like cutting the ear yourself, counts as 'on purpose.' The rule teaches that planning an indirect cause also counts. An example is putting something on the animal's ear so another animal will bite it. Since the person intended the blemish, it is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: indirect causation: setting things up so the damage happens on its own

steps.whatToRemember: The key is intent, not the method. A blemish brought about on purpose is forbidden even when done only indirectly (גרמא).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up גרמא with מִמֵּילָא. In רבא's step, 'by itself' meant no Jew intended or asked for the blemish. In גרמא, the person wanted the blemish and arranged it, so it is forbidden.

phrases.english: It comes to include an indirect cause.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule includes גרמא: an indirectly caused blemish, done with intent, also forbids the animal.

steps.title: 'Without intent' includes someone speaking casually
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the general rule, 'without intent', comes to include a case of מסיח לפי תומו, where the gentile learned about blemishes from a Jew speaking casually, not from a request.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Without intent': this comes to include someone who speaks innocently, without any purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks the same kind of question about the other half of the משנה's rule ('without intent'), and answers it in one breath. It says this phrase comes to include a case of מסיח לפי תומו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Picture a Jew who talks casually and mentions that a blemished בכור may be eaten. A gentile overhears and goes and blemishes the animal. Since the Jew was not trying to get the animal blemished, the animal is permitted, even though the gentile acted on purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: Without intent; the blemish was not planned by the owner
To include; this comes to add another case
Someone speaking innocently, with no hidden purpose

steps.whatToRemember: The general rule has two sides. 'With intent' (לדעת) includes גרמא, which is forbidden. 'Without intent' (שלא לדעת) includes מסיח לפי תומו, which is permitted.
steps.confusionAlert: Who counts here is the Jewish owner, not the gentile. The gentile blemished the animal on purpose, but the owner had no intent, so it is still called 'without intent'.

phrases.english: 'Without intent'
phrases.notes: Quotes the second half of the משנה's general rule. The question 'what does this include?' is understood but not spoken.

phrases.english: comes to include one who speaks innocently.
phrases.notes: The owner spoke casually, without trying to get the animal blemished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to steps 11-12. After explaining what 'with intent' includes, it explains what 'without intent' includes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra case does the phrase 'without intent' add?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It adds מסיח לפי תומו: the gentile acted on a casual remark, so the animal is permitted.

steps.title: New משנה: kicking a בכור that was chasing you
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if a בכור chased its owner and he kicked it, causing a blemish, he may slaughter it because of that blemish.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If a firstborn animal was chasing him, and he kicked it and caused a blemish in it, he may slaughter it on account of that blemish.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that a blemish caused by kicking a בכור that was attacking you is a valid blemish, and the animal may be slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner was defending himself, not trying to make the animal permitted. So this counts as a blemish made without intent to permit the animal. It is a practical example of the 'without intent' side of the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, 'our משנה'; marks the start of a new משנה
Firstborn male animal, which is holy and may not be slaughtered unless it has a blemish
One may slaughter it on account of this blemish

phrases.english: MISHNA:
phrases.notes: A new משנה begins.

phrases.english: If a firstborn animal was chasing him,
and he kicked it and caused a blemish in it,
he may slaughter it on account of that blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה with a fresh case about how a blemish was caused.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blemish caused by kicking an attacking בכור is valid, and the animal may be slaughtered.

steps.title: רב פפא: only a kick during the chase
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא limits the משנה: it is permitted only if he kicked the animal while it was chasing him. A kick after the chase is over does not permit the animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב פפא said: They only taught this when he kicked it at the time of the chase. But after the chase, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רב פפא narrowing the משנה's ruling. It applies only to a kick given during the chase itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: During the chase, the kick is self-defense, so there is no plan to blemish the animal. Once the chase is over, there is no need to defend himself. So a kick then looks like he wanted to blemish it, and the animal is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who adds this limitation
'They only taught it when'; a formula that limits a ruling

phrases.english: GEMARA:
phrases.notes: The גמרא on the new משנה begins.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
They taught this only
where he kicked it at the time of the chase,
but after the chase, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the משנה of step 14 to a kick during the chase.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a kick during the chase permits the בכור. A kick after the chase is treated as intentional, and the animal is forbidden.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: it is obvious that a kick after the chase is not self-defense, so why did he need to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects that רב פפא's limit seems too obvious to need saying. This sets up the next step, which explains what he is adding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה clearly permits the animal because of the chase. Once the chase is over, the reason seems gone. So the גמרא asks what new point רב פפא is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is obvious!'; a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב פפא's statement as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason for permitting is self-defense. After the chase there is clearly no self-defense, so the limit seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: We might have thought it was leftover anger
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא was needed because we might have said a kick after the chase is just anger over the pain he suffered, not a plan to blemish. He teaches that it is still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: he is remembering his pain, and that is why he kicked. So he teaches us that it is still forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'obvious' challenge. Without רב פפא, we might have permitted a kick after the chase as an angry reaction rather than a planned blemish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הוה אמינא is that the owner, still upset from being chased, lashed out in anger, which would count as 'without intent'. רב פפא teaches that we do not assume this. Once the danger has passed, a kick is treated as an intentional blemish, and the animal is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You might have said'; introduces the mistaken first thought (hava amina)
'He teaches us'; introduces the new point being taught

steps.whatToRemember: A kick during the chase is self-defense, and the animal is permitted. A kick after the chase counts as intentional, even if he might have been angry, and the animal is forbidden.

phrases.english: You might have said:
it is his pain that he remembers (so he kicked out of anger);
so he teaches us (that it is forbidden).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge by showing the mistaken first thought that רב פפא rules out.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows a reasonable mistaken first thought that the statement comes to rule out
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A kick after the chase is just anger over the pain he suffered, not a plan, so the animal would be permitted.
steps.terutzMaskana: Once the chase is over, a kick is treated as an intentional blemish, and the בכור may not be slaughtered for it.

steps.title: Second version: even a kick after the chase is permitted
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, רב פפא rules the opposite of the first version. Even a kick after the chase is permitted, because the owner is reacting to the pain he remembers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some report it differently. רב פפא said: Do not think that only a kick during the chase is allowed and a kick not during the chase is forbidden. Even a kick after the chase is also allowed. Why? He is remembering the pain the animal caused him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different report of what רב פפא said. In this report he widens the היתר of the משנה instead of limiting it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version (Steps 15-17), a kick after the chase was forbidden, even though it might come from anger. This version uses that very same idea, that he is upset over his pain, as the reason to permit it. Here the anger shows that he did not plan to make a blemish, so the kick is not a deliberate מום.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say; an alternate version of a statement
The chase (the בכור chasing its owner)

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions agree on the facts: after the chase, the owner may be acting out of anger. They only disagree on whether that anger is enough to permit the animal.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the two versions of רב פפא lead to opposite rulings about a kick after the chase.

phrases.english: There are those who say (a different version):
Rav Pappa said:
Do not say that at the time of the chase, yes (it is permitted),
but not at the time of the chase, no;
rather, even after the chase it is also permitted.
phrases.notes: Read with the words before it: "Do not say only during the chase... rather even after the chase."

phrases.english: What is the reason?
It is his pain that he remembers.
phrases.notes: He kicks out of anger over the pain, not to make a blemish.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא תֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite version of רב פפא's ruling from Steps 15-17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Kicking a chasing בכור, even after the chase, makes a blemish that permits it, because the kick comes from remembered pain and not from a plan.

steps.title: One may blemish a בכור before it is born
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that it is permitted to make a blemish on a בכור before it comes out into the air of the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: It is allowed to put a blemish on a בכור before it has come out into the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. רב יהודה gives a היתר for blemishing a בכור while it is still being born.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally it is forbidden to put a blemish on a בכור. The animal only gets the holiness of a בכור once it is born. Before that, making a blemish is not breaking the איסור, and afterward the animal is blemished and may be slaughtered.

keyTerms.meaning: A firstborn animal that is holy
The air of the world; being born

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a legal way to make a בכור usable by blemishing it before its holiness begins.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
It is permitted to make a blemish in a firstborn
before it has come out into the air of the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: מוּתָּר לְהַטִּיל מוּם בִּבְכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, still about how a בכור becomes blemished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blemishing a בכור before it fully emerges is permitted.

steps.title: Where to make the blemish: a kid's ear, a lamb's lip
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains how to apply רב יהודה's rule. For a kid, blemish its ear. For a lamb, blemish its lip.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A kid, on its ear. A lamb, on its lips.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains how to actually use רב יהודה's היתר. He names which body part comes out first and can be blemished in time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You can only blemish a part of the body that comes out before the animal counts as born. A young goat has long ears that come out ahead of its head. A lamb has short ears, so only its lip comes out early enough.

phrases.english: Rava said:
A kid, on its ear;
phrases.notes: Its long ears come out before the head.

phrases.english: a lamb, on its lips.
phrases.notes: Its ears are short, so only the lip is reachable in time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts רב יהודה's ruling into practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before birth, a kid is blemished on the ear and a lamb on the lip.

steps.title: Second version: a lamb may also be blemished on its ear
steps.stepSummary: Another version of רבא says that a lamb may also be blemished on its ear, because it might come out temples first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: A lamb also on its ear, since we can say it came out by way of its temples.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second report of רבא's practical guidance about the lamb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first version said a lamb's ears never come out early. This version says that a lamb can come out with its temples first, which brings its ears out early. So the ear works for a lamb too.

keyTerms.meaning: We can say; it is possible that

phrases.english: There are those who say:
A lamb also on its ear,
since one may say it came out by way of its temples.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first version of רבא about the lamb.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lamb may also be blemished on its ear, since it may come out temples first.
steps.whatToRemember: Before birth, a בכור may be blemished on a part that comes out early. Everyone agrees a kid's ear works. For a lamb, one version says only the lip works, and another says the ear works too.

steps.title: A mouth blemish that shows only when the animal cries out
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a mouth blemish that cannot be seen while the animal eats, but can be seen when it cries out, counts as a מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If it eats and the blemish is not seen, but it cries out and the blemish is seen, it is a blemish.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new rule about how visible a blemish must be to count as a מום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A blemish must be visible to count. רבא says it is enough if it shows when the animal opens its mouth wide to cry out. It does not need to show during ordinary eating.

phrases.english: Rava said:
When it eats it is not visible,
when it cries out it is visible: it is a blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about how visible a blemish must be.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A mouth blemish that shows only when the animal cries out is a valid מום.

steps.title: Why say it? The משנה about gums already teaches this
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבא adds, since the משנה lists pulled-out inner gums as a blemish. That can only be because they show when the animal cries out.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? We already learned in a משנה: the outer gums that were damaged or scratched, and the inner gums that were pulled out, are blemishes. What is the reason? Is it not because they are seen when it cries out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא for saying something that already seems clear from a משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Inner gums cannot be seen during normal eating, yet the משנה calls them a blemish. The only way they show is when the animal opens its mouth wide to cry out. So the משנה already teaches רבא's rule, and his statement seems unneeded.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (asking what is new)
We already learned this (in a משנה)

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
We already learned:
the outer gums that were damaged or scratched,
the inner ones that were pulled out (are blemishes).
What is the reason?
Is it not because when it cries out it is visible?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's ruling from Step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's statement that a blemish seen only when the animal cries out counts as a מום
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה about pulled-out inner gums already assumes that a blemish seen only during crying out counts, so רבא's statement adds nothing new.

steps.title: רבא is only explaining the reason of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that רבא was not adding a new law. He was explaining why the משנה counts pulled-out inner gums as a blemish.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: רבא too is explaining the reason of the משנה. Why are pulled-out gums a blemish? Because when the animal cries out, it is seen.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge. He changes how we read רבא's statement: it is an explanation, not a new rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed רבא was teaching a new law. רב פפא agrees that the law is already in the משנה. רבא's role is to state the reason behind that משנה, so his words are not wasted.
steps.whatToRemember: A mouth blemish that shows only when the animal cries out is a real מום. This is the reason the משנה counts pulled-out inner gums as a blemish, and רבא was explaining that reason.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Rava too is explaining the reason of the Mishnah:
what is the reason that pulled-out (gums) are a blemish?
Because when it cries out, it is visible.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: רָבָא נָמֵי טַעְמָא דְמַתְנִיתִין מְפָרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the statement is an explanation of the משנה, not a new law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא was teaching a new law that the משנה already contains.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא was explaining the reason behind the משנה's ruling on pulled-out inner gums.

steps.title: Israelite shepherds are believed, priest shepherds are not
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that for blemishes a person could cause, shepherds who are ישראלים are believed, while shepherds who are כהנים are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNA: For any blemish that a person could have made, Israelite shepherds are believed. Priest shepherds are not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It tells us whose word we trust when someone says a בכור's blemish was not made on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making a blemish on a בכור on purpose is forbidden, but a blemished בכור can be eaten outside the בית המקדש. A כהן who gets the בכור gains if it is blemished, so the משנה does not trust כהנים here. A ישראל does not gain the same way, so he is trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: Blemishes: physical defects that disqualify an animal from being a קרבן
Blemishes that a person could have caused
Shepherds who are ישראלים, not כהנים

steps.confusionAlert: Only blemishes a person COULD make are in question. If a blemish could never be man-made, nobody needs to be believed about it.

phrases.english: MISHNA: All the blemishes
that could be brought about by a person
Israelite shepherds are believed
phrases.notes: They are believed when they say the blemish was not made on purpose.

phrases.english: priest shepherds are not believed
phrases.notes: A כהן gains from a blemished בכור, so he has a motive to lie.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ כׇּל הַמּוּמִין הָרְאוּיִין לָבֹא בִּידֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It moves from how a blemish may be made to who is trusted about how a blemish came about.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For blemishes a person could cause, ישראל shepherds are believed and כהן shepherds are not.

steps.title: A priest is believed about someone else's animal
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says a כהן is believed about another person's בכור but not about his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: He is believed about his friend's animal, but not believed about his own.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the משנה narrows the rule. Only a כהן testifying about his own animal is not trusted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion distrusts כהן shepherds in general. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the problem is only personal gain. If the בכור is not his, the כהן gets nothing from his testimony, so he is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא, נשיא of the generation
Belonging to his fellow, someone else's

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says
he is believed about his fellow's animal
and he is not believed about his own

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a narrower view than the first opinion in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן is believed about another's בכור but not about his own.

steps.title: A suspected person may not judge or testify
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says one who is suspect in a matter can neither judge it nor testify about it, even for others.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: One who is suspected about a matter may not judge it and may not testify about it.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion in the משנה is stricter than רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. A suspected person is not trusted on this subject at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר does not care whose animal it is. If a person is suspected of making blemishes, he loses his trust for this whole subject. He cannot rule as a judge on it and cannot testify about it, even about another person's animal.

keyTerms.meaning: One who is suspected regarding a matter

steps.whyThisMatters: רבי מאיר's line, "החשוד על הדבר לא דנו ולא מעידו", becomes a general principle about trust and suspicion used across many areas.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says
one who is suspected regarding the matter
may neither judge it nor testify about it
phrases.notes: This holds even when the case is about someone else's animal.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: הֶחָשׁוּד עַל הַדֶּבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and is stricter.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person suspected in a matter may neither judge it nor testify about it.

steps.title: Israelite shepherds working for priests are believed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר disagree about the משנה. One explains that "Israelite shepherds" means ישראלים working for a כהן. They are believed, and we do not worry they would lie for a bite of meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר disagree. One says: "Israelite shepherds" means those working in the house of priests. They are believed. We are not worried about a swallow of meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a dispute about how to read the משנה. The first opinion explains that the משנה is speaking about who the shepherd works for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think a ישראל working for a כהן would lie so his boss gives him a taste of the בכור meat. This opinion says such a small gain is not enough to suspect him. So he is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: The house of priests, meaning in their employ
For a swallow, a small taste

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not tell us which of the two (רבי יוחנן or רבי אלעזר) holds this view. The other opinion is given in step 33.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree
one says: "Israelite shepherds" means those in the house of priests
are believed; we are not concerned about a swallow
phrases.notes: Concern that the כהן boss might give them a taste of the meat is not a reason to suspect them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's explanation of the משנה's first ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ישראל shepherd working for a כהן is believed. A small taste of meat is not a reason to suspect him.

steps.title: Priest shepherds working for an Israelite are not believed
steps.stepSummary: The same opinion explains that "priest shepherds" means כהנים working for a ישראל. They are not believed, because the כהן expects the owner to give him the בכור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Priest shepherds in the house of an Israelite are not believed. He says to himself: since I worked hard with it, the owner will not leave me out and give it to someone else.
steps.whatsHappening: The same opinion now explains the second half of the משנה. It shows why the כהן shepherd has a real motive to lie.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ישראל may give his בכור to any כהן he chooses. The כהן shepherd expects that the owner will give it to him, since he took care of it. So he gains a whole animal if it is blemished, and he is not trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: He says to himself, he thinks

phrases.english: priest shepherds in the house of an Israelite
are not believed
because he says to himself
since I have worked hard with it
he will not leave me out
and give it to others

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the first opinion's reading by explaining the second half of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן shepherd working for a ישראל is not believed, because he expects to receive the בכור.

steps.title: A priest testifying for another priest is also not believed
steps.stepSummary: The same opinion adds that one כהן is not believed for another כהן, because we worry they will do favors for each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the same is true for a priest testifying for a priest, because we are concerned about paying back favors.
steps.whatsHappening: The opinion widens its rule to another case. A כהן is not trusted even about another כהן's בכור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the testifying כהן gets nothing right now. But the other כהן may later lie for him in return. This hidden two-way gain is enough to distrust him, which differs from רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who trusts a כהן about another's animal.

keyTerms.meaning: Paying back, returning favors to each other

steps.whatToRemember: According to this first opinion, the משנה is about who employs the shepherd. A small taste of meat does not make someone suspect. Expecting the whole בכור does. Even trading favors between כהנים makes a כהן suspect.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a delayed, indirect gain, such as a favor paid back later, can still remove a witness's trust.

phrases.english: and the same is true for a priest for a priest
because we are concerned about paying back favors
phrases.notes: The other כהן might later lie for him in return.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the first opinion's rule to a כהן testifying for another כהן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן is not believed for another כהן, because of the worry that they will repay each other's favors.

steps.title: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view within the first explanation
steps.stepSummary: Under the first explanation, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the תנא קמא. He holds that a כהן is believed about another כהן's בכור, but not about his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבן שמעון בן גמליאל comes to say: a כהן is believed about his friend's בכור, but he is not believed about his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still inside the first explanation of the משנה. It now shows what רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds to the picture.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 30, the first view said one כהן is not believed for another כהן, because they might do favors for each other. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל does not worry about that kind of favor-trading. He only suspects a כהן about his own בכור, where he gains directly.

keyTerms.meaning: And [he] comes to say. The גמרא uses this to show what each opinion adds.
That of his fellow (here, another כהן's בכור)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not just a repeat of Step 26. The גמרא is now placing רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's words inside the first אמורא's reading of the משנה, as a direct argument against the worry about כהנים doing favors for each other in Step 30.

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲתָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל לְמֵימַר:
phrases.english: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel comes to say:
he is believed about that of his fellow,
phrases.notes: A כהן testifying about another כהן's firstborn.

phrases.english: but he is not believed about his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲתָא רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the first explanation. It shows that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל rejects Step 30's worry about כהנים doing favors for each other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן is believed about another כהן's בכור, but not about his own.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's stricter view within the first explanation
steps.stepSummary: Under the first explanation, רבי מאיר adds a broad rule. Anyone suspect about a matter may neither judge it nor testify about it, even for other people.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מאיר comes to say: one who is suspect about a matter may not judge it and may not testify about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the first explanation by showing where רבי מאיר fits. He is the strictest opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל only suspects a כהן about his own בכור. רבי מאיר goes much further. Once someone is suspect in an area, he is disqualified from judging or testifying in that whole area, even when he gains nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: One who is suspect about the matter
And he may not testify about it

steps.whatToRemember: Under the first explanation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that a כהן is believed for another כהן but not for himself. The תנא קמא holds that a כהן is not believed even for another כהן, because of mutual favors. רבי מאיר holds that someone suspect may neither judge nor testify in that matter. This amud does not yet explain how רבי מאיר's ruling differs from the תנא קמא's.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir comes to say:
one who is suspect about the matter
may neither judge it nor testify about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the first explanation by placing רבי מאיר's broad disqualification rule within it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone suspect in a matter is disqualified from both judging and testifying in it, even for others.

steps.title: The second explanation: Israelite shepherds are כהנים
steps.stepSummary: The other אמורא reads 'רועי ישראל' as shepherds who are כהנים working for a ישראל. He says they are believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one says: 'Israelite shepherds' means the shepherds are כהנים (working for a ישראל), and they are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the second אמורא's explanation of the משנה. This opens a new reading that disagrees with the first one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first view (Step 29), כהנים working for a ישראל were not believed. They expect the owner to give them the בכור, so they might lie. This second view says the opposite: such כהנים are believed. We do not suspect them of lying just to get the meat.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one says. This introduces the second side of a disagreement between אמוראים.
Shepherds of Israelites, meaning they tend a ישראל's flock

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'רועי ישראל' does NOT mean shepherds who are ישראלים. It means shepherds of a ישראל's animals, and the shepherds themselves are כהנים. This is the exact opposite of how the first explanation read the phrase.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two אמוראים argue over the same case: כהנים working for a ישראל. One says they are not believed, and the other says they are. This shows they disagree about how much a כהן's hope of getting the בכור makes him suspect.

phrases.english: And the other one says: 'Israelite shepherds'
where they are priests — are believed,
phrases.notes: These are כהנים working for a ישראל owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the second אמורא's explanation. It directly reverses Step 29's ruling on כהנים working for a ישראל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כהנים working for a ישראל are believed about blemishes on the owner's בכור.
